title: Scale‐dependent pathways from land use to fish diversity: eDNA analysis reveals water quality as key mediator in the Nanliu River Basin
content:
Abstract

Human-induced land-use change poses substantial risks to aquatic biodiversity; however, the multi-scale pathways linking land-use patterns to fish diversity remain insufficiently resolved. Focusing on the Nanliu River Basin (Guangxi, China), we integrated environmental DNA (eDNA) detection with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) across three spatial scales—1000 m circular buffers, 2000 m river (riparian) buffers, and sub-watersheds—to quantify the effects on species richness, Shannon diversity, and Simpson diversity. We detected 36 fish species, dominated by Cypriniformes (45.8%). At the local scale (1000 m circular buffer), fish diversity was promoted indirectly via landscape configuration (landscape→diversity 0.343), which was strengthened by a higher water body proportion. Land use positively shaped landscape configuration (0.617) but degraded water quality (land use→water quality –0.422), with TN and TP as major negative contributors and a weak direct water quality →diversity path (–0.079). At the riparian scale (2000 m river buffer), water quality—proxied by electrical conductivity—was the primary positive driver of diversity (0.329). Land use affected diversity indirectly via water-body proportion and a secondary pathway through landscape configuration (0.197), whereas the direct landscape→diversity effect was minimal (–0.021). At the sub-watershed scale, TP exerted a strong negative influence on diversity (–0.474); land use acted via nested mediation through water body proportion and landscape configuration (0.416), and the direct landscape→diversity path was negative (–0.098). Fish communities showed pronounced spatial heterogeneity, with the highest diversity in estuaries (Shannon = 3.31, Simpson = 0.92, richness = 18) and the lowest in urban sections (Shannon = 1.94, Simpson = 0.68, richness = 5). Collectively, the models support a scale-dependent mechanism—land use → landscape pattern → water quality → fish diversity—and provide a quantitative basis for spatially targeted biodiversity conservation and watershed ecological management in subtropical river basins.
